title: Durability
description: Follow committed data through logging, crashes, and recovery, and distinguish InnoDB durability settings from replication and backup guarantees.

questions.question_text: What does durability promise after a successful commit under the documented configuration and storage assumptions?
options: Fast transaction commits
Committed changes survive the failures covered by that documented guarantee
Transactions never fail
Data is always encrypted at rest
questions.explanation: Durability is scoped to a failure model and persistence assumptions; it does not promise survival after every possible disaster.

questions.question_text: Does durability require an unfinished transaction to survive as committed business work after a pre-commit crash?
options: Yes, its partial changes are preserved
No; unfinished physical changes may need undo or exclusion during atomic recovery
It guarantees the transaction will automatically retry
Durability guarantees the crash never happened
questions.explanation: Durability protects committed outcomes. Unfinished work can already have physical effects, but recovery must not present it as a completed business transaction.

questions.question_text: What mechanism typically helps provide durability?
options: An in-memory cache with no disk involvement
A write-ahead log (Chapter 26) that records changes durably before/alongside the commit
Deleting old data to save space
Running the database in read-only mode
questions.explanation: Write-ahead logging is the standard mechanism for achieving durable commits, covered further in Chapter 26.

questions.question_text: Can a database be configured to trade away some durability for higher write performance?
options: No, durability is always absolute with no configuration
Yes — some systems offer weaker durability modes as an explicit performance trade-off, a genuine configuration risk when enabled
This would violate the SQL standard and is never possible
Durability can only be strengthened, never weakened
questions.explanation: Configurable durability trade-offs exist in some real systems, worth understanding as an explicit choice.

questions.question_text: Can durability be violated even if the database software behaves correctly?
options: No, durability is guaranteed purely by database software logic
Yes — a genuinely faulty disk or a storage layer that lies about a write succeeding can violate durability despite correct database behavior
Only a database bug can violate durability
Durability is guaranteed regardless of the physical storage medium
questions.explanation: Durability ultimately depends on the physical storage actually behaving as promised, which is outside the database's own control.

questions.question_text: Why do some real systems add replication or checksums beyond a single disk's guarantees?
options: These have nothing to do with durability
As extra safeguards against physical storage failures that could otherwise violate durability
To make transactions commit faster
To reduce the need for isolation
questions.explanation: Extra redundancy compensates for the risk that a single storage medium's own guarantee might not hold.

questions.question_text: What supports relying on an acknowledged successful COMMIT within the system’s documented failure model?
options: Nothing — commits can be silently undone at any time
Durability, provided the configured persistence policy and storage assumptions satisfy that model
Atomicity alone, without needing Durability
The absence of any storage medium involvement
questions.explanation: The promise concerns covered failures and the actual durability configuration, rather than unconditional permanence under every failure.

questions.question_text: Is durability a guarantee about IN-PROGRESS (uncommitted) transaction state?
options: Yes, all in-progress state is durable
No — durability specifically concerns state AFTER a successful commit, not in-progress uncommitted work
Durability applies equally to both committed and uncommitted state
In-progress state is irrelevant to any ACID property
questions.explanation: Durability's guarantee is scoped strictly to the post-commit state.

questions.question_text: What is the central durability promise?
options: Committed effects survive failures covered by the guarantee
All unfinished work must survive
Every replica is always current
Every query is always available
questions.explanation: Durability concerns retained committed state under a specified failure model.

questions.question_text: Can a committed change survive when its data page was not flushed before a crash?
options: No, data pages must always be forced per commit
Yes, recovery can redo it from durable logging
Only if the table has no key
Only if it was a SELECT
questions.explanation: Recovery logs allow committed cached changes to be reconstructed.

questions.question_text: In the simplified trace, T commits A=130 and U writes B=55 without committing. What is the recovery goal from A=100, B=40?
questions.explanation: T is committed while U must not appear as a completed transaction.

questions.question_text: What does redo information support?
options: Sending emails
Choosing candidate keys
Reapplying changes required during recovery
Removing every index
questions.explanation: Redo supports reconstruction of logged changes as required by recovery.

questions.question_text: Why specify a failure model?
options: All failures have identical effects
COMMIT prevents all disasters
Backups cover zero recent data loss automatically
Process crash and total storage loss require different protection
questions.explanation: A guarantee must identify the failures it covers.

questions.question_text: Which InnoDB setting controls redo write and flush timing at commit?
options: innodb_flush_log_at_trx_commit
group_concat_max_len
sql_safe_updates
max_sort_length
questions.explanation: The redo durability policy is controlled by innodb_flush_log_at_trx_commit.

questions.question_text: Why is a periodic flush interval not a precise loss bound?
options: SQL timestamps are always strings
Scheduling and system behavior affect actual timing
Redo logs cannot contain time
All flushes are instantaneous
questions.explanation: A configured interval is not proof of an exact maximum loss window.

questions.question_text: Does source local durability imply an asynchronous replica has every acknowledged write?
options: Yes, by definition
Only if rows are ordered
No, replication may lag
Yes, whenever a backup exists
questions.explanation: Local persistence and replica acknowledgment are separate properties.

questions.question_text: What does recovery point objective describe?
options: Maximum SQL identifier length
The number of table indexes
Transaction isolation level
Acceptable data loss
questions.explanation: Recovery point objective concerns the acceptable gap in recovered data.

questions.question_text: A commit succeeds but its acknowledgment is lost. Which statement is correct?
options: The data can be durable while the client is uncertain
The data certainly vanished
The transaction never began
The client should always duplicate the operation
questions.explanation: Persistent outcome and client knowledge are distinct.

questions.question_text: Why test backup restoration?
options: Restoration disables durability
A stored backup alone does not prove recoverability
Backups never contain data
Testing replaces all log retention
questions.explanation: Usable recovery requires working restoration procedures and required artifacts.

questions.question_text: Which observation proves only a narrower property than power loss survival?
options: A destructive power failure test with defined evidence
A documented storage flush guarantee
A normal local database restart preserves a row
A validated disaster recovery exercise
questions.explanation: A graceful or ordinary restart does not exercise every physical failure mode.

notes:
## The promise after commit

Durability means that a transaction reported as committed remains part of the database state after the failures covered by the system's durability guarantee. A student pays an application fee and receives a successful receipt. Restarting the database should not erase the recorded payment. This property begins at the successful commit decision; it does not mean unfinished work must survive, and it does not mean every possible disaster is covered without backups or replication.

The practical question is precise: which failures are covered, and when may the system acknowledge success? A database process crash, an operating system crash, loss of power, and destruction of every storage device are different failure models. Surviving the first does not prove survival of the last. Storage configuration, software settings, hardware behavior, replication policy, and recovery procedures all contribute to the actual promise. Treat durability as a documented contract with an explicit failure model.

## Separate memory from persistent state

A database commonly modifies cached pages in memory before writing those pages to their final data files. Flushing every changed page for every transaction would be expensive and would interfere with useful batching. Recovery logging allows the system to acknowledge a transaction once the necessary recovery information has reached the required persistent boundary, even when some data pages are still dirty in memory. The database can later reconstruct the committed state from that information.

Write ahead logging requires the relevant log records to reach stable storage before corresponding dirty data pages are persisted in a way that would prevent correct recovery. A commit record identifies a completed transaction in a simplified recovery model. Redo information supports reapplying committed changes not yet present in data pages. Undo information supports removing incomplete work where the recovery design requires it. Actual engine recovery algorithms are more detailed than this teaching model, so do not infer an engine's exact file format from the notation.

## Follow a small recovery example

Suppose an account contains 100 credits. Transaction T changes it to 130 and commits. A simplified log contains a record for the change and a durable commit record. The database crashes before the data page containing 130 reaches its final file location. Recovery sees that T committed and restores the committed effect as necessary. The account is 130 after recovery. The change does not become optional merely because the final data page was still cached at the instant of failure.

Now consider transaction U, which changes a different account from 40 to 55 but has no durable commit decision when the crash occurs. The recovery outcome must not present U as successfully committed. Depending on the engine's algorithm, its effects may be undone or ignored as incomplete. The expected committed database state contains T's 130 and excludes U's unfinished increment. This distinction connects durability to [atomicity](/learning/dbms-sql-tutorial/atomicity), but the two properties answer different questions.

```text
Initial: A=100, B=40
T: write A=130
T: durable commit
U: write B=55
Crash before U commits
Recovery goal: A=130, B=40
```

This is a reasoning trace rather than an executable crash test. It deliberately abstracts away page identifiers, log sequence numbers, checkpoints, and undo chains. Its value is that it forces the learner to identify which transaction crossed the commit boundary. Merely inspecting which value happened to reach a data page cannot determine the correct logical outcome because uncommitted pages and committed cached changes can coexist in real recovery designs.

## MySQL InnoDB durability settings

MySQL InnoDB uses redo logging, and its commit durability behavior depends on documented configuration. The innodb_flush_log_at_trx_commit setting controls when redo is written and flushed. The value 1 writes and flushes redo at transaction commit. Values 0 and 2 relax parts of this behavior and can lose recent committed transactions under specified failures. Periodic flushing should not be interpreted as a precise maximum loss interval because scheduling and system behavior affect timing.

When binary logging is enabled, durability of that log is a separate concern relevant to replication and point in time recovery. The sync_binlog setting controls its synchronization policy. Redo and binary logs serve different purposes; preserving one does not automatically prove the other's durability. This lesson explains the settings so a reader can ask the right operational questions. It does not recommend changing a live configuration or claim that one parameter alone makes unreliable hardware safe.

The storage stack must honor flush requests correctly. A volatile device cache that reports data safe before it is protected can defeat assumptions made by the database. Conversely, protected caches and reliable persistent storage can support the intended guarantee. Assess the complete stack rather than equating an SQL COMMIT statement with a physical proof of power loss survival. Documentation and controlled testing complement each other; neither a code snippet nor a successful SELECT proves the hardware failure model.

## Distinguish durability from availability and backup

Durability does not guarantee that a database is currently reachable. A committed record may remain intact while a server is temporarily unavailable. A replica can improve availability, but asynchronous replication can lag behind acknowledged writes. Promoting that replica after source failure can therefore expose data loss unless the configured protocol and failover procedure provide a stronger guarantee. Ask which replica has acknowledged which state before treating replication as a durability claim.

Backups protect against a different class of failure, including some disasters and operator mistakes. A backup from yesterday does not preserve a payment committed this morning unless suitable log retention and recovery procedures bridge the gap. Recovery point objective describes acceptable data loss; recovery time objective describes acceptable restoration time. These objectives should match business requirements. A long retained history is useful only when restoration has actually been exercised and the necessary keys and logs remain available through approved operational processes.

## Application consequences

A client can lose the connection after the server commits but before the acknowledgment arrives. Durability and client certainty then diverge: the record can be safely stored while the caller does not know whether its request succeeded. Blind retry can duplicate an operation. Use a business operation identifier and a reliable outcome lookup so the caller can reconcile uncertain results. The database cannot infer that two independently identified payment requests represent the same intended action.

Do not use the presence of a success message in application memory as the authoritative durability record. Record the business result in the transaction and acknowledge according to the actual commit outcome. For side effects such as email, distinguish the durable intent to send from delivery itself. A database restart test can check an important behavior in a local environment, but that evidence remains narrower than a power cut test or a regional disaster recovery exercise.

## Exercises with recovery explanations

Exercise one: a committed update is absent from its final data page, but the required durable log records survive. Is the update necessarily lost? No. Recovery can redo the committed effect. The purpose of recovery logging is precisely to avoid requiring every changed data page to be forced at each commit. Check the engine's documented recovery behavior before making stronger claims about a particular installation.

Exercise two: a transaction changes A and B, then the database crashes before commit. Should recovery preserve just A because that page reached disk? No. That would expose a partially completed transaction. The correct logical outcome excludes the unfinished transaction as a committed action. Physical write order alone does not define the business result. Atomicity and recovery rules must restore a valid committed state.

Exercise three: an asynchronous replica is missing the newest five committed orders when the source becomes unavailable. Does the source's durable commit guarantee that immediate replica promotion contains those orders? No. Local durability does not imply replication acknowledgment. The recovery decision requires evidence about replication position, the surviving source storage, and the accepted recovery objective. Study [transaction boundaries](/learning/dbms-sql-tutorial/transaction-boundaries) to connect acknowledgment and retry design with the database's commit decision.
